name: Arab fascism
summary: Arab fascism combined Arab ultranationalism with fascist forms: a leader principle, uniformed paramilitary youth, anti-parliamentary politics, militarism and expansionist unity claims. It grew in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Egypt between the wars, drew on Italian and German support, and in parts turned strongly antisemitic, especially around the 1941 Farhud and after 1948. Economics were state-nationalist and anti-capitalist; attitudes to Islam ranged from Islamic-nationalist to secular.
scope: The interwar pan-Arab movements the Wikipedia article treats as Arab fascism: Sami Shawkat's Iraqi Al-Futuwwa and the Muthanna Club, Egypt's Young Egypt (Green Shirts) and the early pan-Arab nationalism that fed Ba'athism, with the 1947 Ba'th constitution used for economic and unity positions. Michel Aflaq's later Ba'ath is only a neighbour, and the Syrian Social Nationalist Party is excluded as a core case because Saadeh rejected Arabism and fascism and was secular. Later regimes (Saddam Hussein, Janjaweed/RSF) are excluded.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Not a focus of the interwar movements, but the 1947 Ba'th constitution guarantees social security and state-run social provision, so a state-guaranteed service fits a statist nationalism.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th constitution's demand that wages give a decent living standard and ban exploitation of labor; the fascist-style youth movements issued no wage programme.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Young Egypt was anti-capitalist and economically protectionist, and the Ba'th constitution puts major resources under national ownership and state control of trade, so state direction beats free markets.

public-ownership.rationale: The 1947 Ba'th constitution makes natural resources, large-scale production and transport national property run by the state; Young Egypt favoured national economic control against foreign firms.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th constitution's statement that the present distribution of wealth is unjust and from Young Egypt's anti-capitalism; no tax programme is documented.

unions-good.rationale: The Ba'th constitution promises free unions for workers and peasants, but the paramilitary nationalist strands subordinated class bodies to the nation, so adherents are split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Ba'th text calls property and inheritance natural rights but limited by the national interest, with land and holdings capped, so property can readily be overridden.

regulate-corporations.rationale: State supervision of trade and ownership of major enterprises is in the Ba'th constitution, and Young Egypt attacked foreign-owned firms and capital.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred: a corporate, paternalist nationalism stressing social security and the family has no case against welfare, though no programme is documented.

worker-ownership.rationale: Ba'th text gives workers a share in management and profits but keeps major industry nationally owned; the fascist-inspired movements rejected worker control as class politics.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Inferred from authoritarian, security-state practice of Ba'thist regimes and a doctrine that the party decides the common good; no explicit statement on terrorism.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from Young Egypt's campaign against gambling, alcohol and 'anti-Islamic' vices and a morally disciplinary youth ethos.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Inferred: the movements spread antisemitic propaganda and censored opponents, so they would not accept speech limits protecting minorities, though they limited speech for national interest.

strong-leader.rationale: Arab fascism is defined by a leader principle; Futuwwa and Muthanna Club copied European fascist leadership and youth models, and Young Egypt was run around Ahmad Hussein as a fiery leader.

state-harmful.rationale: A fascist-style pan-Arab movement exalts a strong state; the Ba'th constitution gives the state broad ownership and direction of the economy and education.

limit-guns.rationale: Paramilitary groups armed their own members, but regimes monopolised arms; adherents would back party/state arms control while rejecting general civilian ownership.

empower-police-military.rationale: Militarism and paramilitary youth drill (Futuwwa, Green Shirts) are core features, and the Ba'th text makes military service compulsory.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Young Egypt campaigned against moral vice; inferred from its puritanical nationalist ethos.

decide-locally.rationale: The Ba'th constitution calls for administrative decentralisation, but the movements prized unity under one centralised nationalist leadership, so local decision-making is not central.

rehabilitation.rationale: Inferred from the militarist, discipline-oriented ethos; no penal policy is documented.

traditional-family.rationale: The Ba'th constitution calls the family the basic cell of the nation, which the state should protect, and Young Egypt defended Egypt's moral culture.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Young Egypt attacked 'anti-Islamic' morals and the movements shared conservative sexual norms; recognition of same-sex marriage is far outside their outlook.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th constitution's pronatal family policy treating marriage and children as national duties.

more-religion-public.rationale: The article says some adherents were Arab-Islamic nationalists and others secular; Young Egypt wanted religion in public morals while Aflaq wanted it kept out of the state.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Inferred: an ethnically defined nationalism has no tradition of redress programmes for historic racial injustice.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from the family-centred, traditional view in Ba'th and Young Egypt texts, though Ba'th claims full civic rights for women.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Ba'th Education Article 1 requires a national Arab character in education linking pupils to their history, and Young Egypt demanded rejection of foreign influence.

gradual-change.rationale: The 1947 Ba'th constitution says goals can be reached only through upheaval and struggle and rejects gradual reform.

reduce-immigration.rationale: No documented position on immigration; Ba'th would admit any Arab and expel anti-Arab racist or colonial settlers, so the answer depends on who immigrates.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Anti-colonial nationalists distrusted League-style bodies that preserved colonial borders; Aflaq criticised the Arab League for reinforcing existing states.

free-trade.rationale: Young Egypt promoted buying only Egyptian goods and the Ba'th text has the state supervise trade and protect national production.

nation-first.rationale: Ultranationalism is the defining trait; the Ba'th constitution subordinates regional interests to the wider Arab national interest and treats colonialism as a crime.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Interventions by Western powers were seen as colonialism, which the Ba'th text says must be fought by every means.

open-borders.rationale: Fascist-style nationalism rejects open borders; even the pan-Arab ideal is a single Arab state, not borderless humanity.

limit-growth.rationale: Inferred from the movements' emphasis on national strength and development through national ownership and industrialisation.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; no documented position, and development priorities compete with state-directed action.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Inferred from modernising national-development aims (Young Egypt's industry drives, Ba'th renaissance), though no direct statement.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from a national-strength and self-sufficiency outlook favouring independent national power.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Ba'th constitution states that aims are reached only through upheaval and struggle, and Aflaq's strategy was seizing power state by state.

experts-over-public.rationale: Aflaq's vanguard party decided the common good against majority opinion, but this rests on party elite, not technocratic experts.

central-planning.rationale: The Ba'th constitution has the state own major production and supervise trade, which points to state planning, though the early fascist-style groups gave no detailed plan.

socialized-markets.rationale: Ba'th mixed state ownership with capped private property; the fascist-style strands gave no stance on worker-owned markets.

land-value-tax.rationale: No documented position; Ba'th caps land holdings instead, so this tax is not a concern.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Ba'th text calls inheritance a natural right limited by national interest, which allows limits but not heavy taxation per se.

basic-income.rationale: Inferred: the Ba'th text makes work compulsory for the able, which sits badly with unconditional payments.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Young Egypt's buy-Egyptian drive and the Ba'th provision protecting national production back protectionism.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State ownership of major production and control of trade in the Ba'th text imply the state steers strategic investment.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Ba'th text guarantees a minimum holding and caps large holdings, which resembles this, but the nationalist movements did not centre it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Ba'th text makes work compulsory and sets decent wages; abolishing wage labor is a Marxist aim Aflaq rejected.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Ba'th proposes a single state bank issuing currency, the opposite of market money, though central banking would be nationalised, not abolished.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Fascist-style corporatism is typical of the type, and the Ba'th text offers workers shared management and state-regulated labor relations.

one-party-rule.rationale: Ba'athism favoured one-party states and a vanguard party acting for the common good; Young Egypt and Futuwwa pursued mass-party leadership.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Ba'th revolution opposed feudalism and reaction; Futuwwa and Muthanna Club plotted against British-backed monarchy, while Young Egypt courted the king, so views split but lean against.

democracy-best.rationale: Aflaq called liberal democracy unsuitable and favoured a non-elected party guaranteeing liberty; the movements attacked the parliamentary politics of the Wafd.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred from the leader-centred, anti-parliamentary outlook; no plebiscite programme is documented.

workers-councils.rationale: Aflaq rejected class struggle and Marxist politics; workers' councils as the basis of power conflicts with party and leader rule.

right-to-secede.rationale: Pan-Arab unity into one state is the primary goal; the Ba'th text bars regionalism and particularism.

natural-rulers.rationale: Fascist-style hierarchies and the leader principle imply it, though the sources do not state a doctrine of natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Ba'th text says goals need upheaval and struggle; Young Egypt's attack on Nahas and the Farhud involved Futuwwa members.

war-builds-character.rationale: Anti-rationalism and cult of strength; Shawkat's Futuwwa taught sacrifice and military virtue, per the Arab fascism article.

separate-church-state.rationale: Split: Aflaq wanted Islam kept out of the state and the SSNP was secular, while Young Egypt and Arab-Islamic nationalists wanted a religious public order.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Some adherents were Islamist-leaning, but the mainstream was a nationalist ideology that made the nation, not scripture, the source of law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: A statist nationalism puts courts and defence in the state's hands; the Ba'th constitution has an independent state judiciary and compulsory service.

military-superiority.rationale: Militarism and expansionism are core to the type, and Futuwwa trained youth for war.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The Ba'th constitution defines the nation by Arab language and belonging, and expels anti-Arab racist groups, so the nation is Arab, not necessarily ethnically pure.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Aflaq rejected class struggle as divisive and held all Arab classes united against foreign capitalism, and fascist-style groups rejected class-based history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Ba'th corrects unjust distribution of wealth but the movements prized national hierarchy; equality of outcomes is not a stated aim.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed; anti-colonial but ethnically Arab-centred, so a split.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th text describing colonialism as a crime and demanding cancellation of concessions.

civilizational-union.rationale: The first principle of the 1947 Ba'th constitution makes the Arab nation one political and economic unit seeking a single state.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Fascist-style anti-individualism subordinates self-interest to the nation.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Anti-liberal, collectivist movements put the nation first; the Ba'th text limits freedoms to the Arab national interest.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The interwar movements said nothing about nature's intrinsic worth; a nationalist, development-minded outlook gives no basis for either side.

limit-population.rationale: The Ba'th text frames marriage and children as a national duty, which opposes limiting births.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movements pursued national strengthening and industrialisation, opposing any reversal.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred from modernising, national-strength aims, but their traditional culture attacks disruption of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from a morally conservative outlook.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; leader-centred authority is incompatible with rule by algorithms.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the police-state practice of Ba'thist regimes, which would not want citizens beyond state reach.

restore-past-order.rationale: Ba'th stressed renaissance, a rebirth of past Arab greatness in new form, not restoration of a particular order; Young Egypt and others combined both.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movements were ideological and emotional, anti-rationalist and anti-intellectual per the Arab fascism article.

direct-action.rationale: Green Shirts and Futuwwa pursued street demonstration, paramilitary force and attempted assassination rather than parliamentary methods.

means-match-ends.rationale: Fascist-style groups justified authoritarian means for national ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: These movements sought national strength through industry, schooling and military training (Ba'th Educ. Arts 2-4), so a return to foraging is far outside their programme.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The Ba'th text organises labor, unions and wages, not abolition of the division of labor.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The Ba'th text pays wages for work and makes work compulsory, so distribution by work, not need.

production-for-use.rationale: Ba'th socialism nationalises key production but the groups did not frame it this way.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Ba'th bans exploitation of others' labor and gives workers a profit share, but rejects Marxist class analysis.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Aflaq rejected class struggle and Marxist dialectical materialism, and fascist-style movements were anticommunist.

collective-farming.rationale: The 1947 text caps holdings by personal cultivation; collective farming came only in the 1963 text.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Aflaq blamed foreign capitalism for domination, but the groups did not endorse the Marxist theory.

taxation-theft.rationale: A statist nationalism that owns major industry and runs education and social security (Ba'th constitution) treats taxation as a legitimate state power.

harm-principle.rationale: The Ba'th text limits freedoms by the Arab national interest, and the movements policed morals.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Anti-liberal collectivism treats the nation as the bearer of rights.

conscription.rationale: Ba'th Internal Article 8 makes military service compulsory, and Futuwwa militarised youth.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Statist and nationalist; leaving a state is not a check on government.

state-as-business.rationale: Statist and anti-capitalist; citizens are members of a nation, not customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: Ba'th text promises employment, education and social provision as conditions of freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: No position documented; Young Egypt was a student-led movement, which cuts against treating universities as the ruling power.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Some adherents admired Nazi race ideas, but Hussein and others grew sceptical and Ba'th defines Arabs by language; a split leaning mildly positive.

organic-representation.rationale: Fascist-style corporatism implies representation through bodies of work, though the Ba'th text promises elections and a constitution.

total-state.rationale: The type seeks total mobilisation, but the Ba'th text allows freedoms of speech and belief within the national interest, so not fully total.

national-rebirth.rationale: Baath means renaissance, the core idea of Aflaq's ideology; the Ba'th text calls for upheaval to revive the Arab nation.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The article says Futuwwa, Young Egypt and the SSNP shared expansionist goals, and Shawkat promoted an expansionist Arab nation.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Loyalty to a leader is central, but feudal-style oaths were opposed as feudalism by the Ba'th text.

bound-labor.rationale: The Ba'th text abolishes feudalism's burdens and sets land by personal cultivation.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The article notes anti-rationalism and anti-intellectualism, but no documented claim about knowledge reflecting power.

universal-morality.rationale: Nationalist, anti-rationalist outlook; no universalism documented.

single-common-good.rationale: Aflaq's party acted for one common good against majority opinion, rejecting pluralism.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The article says the movements became increasingly antisemitic after Israel's establishment, and Arab nationalism opposed Zionism.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The Ba'th text calls on Arab emigrants to ties with the homeland, but no general doctrine is documented.

revive-national-language.rationale: Arabic as the sole official language is in the Ba'th text; revival of lost language is inapplicable.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Ba'th text gives workers a share in management and profits, but fascist-style groups rejected democratic control.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Ba'th text makes education a state responsibility and abolishes private schools.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: State control of the economy suggests tolerating state-led spending.

economic-freedom.rationale: Aflaq treated liberty as guaranteed by the party, not as dependent on economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Cult of the leader and moral exemplar; no documented policy.

national-self-determination.rationale: The first principle says Arabs form a nation with a natural right to a state of their own.

force-without-un.rationale: Expansionist militarism; no need for approval by an international body.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The article lists anti-rationalism and emotional appeal as shared traits.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Ba'th limits civil rights to loyal citizens on Arab soil; inferred preference for citizens.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The Ba'th constitution makes work compulsory for those able to do it while guaranteeing jobs and social security, so benefits tied to work fit.

class-collaboration.rationale: Aflaq held all Arab classes united against foreign capitalism and rejected class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Ba'th education ties pupils to their history, and Young Egypt prized tradition.

dominated-front.rationale: The Ba'th text calls colonialism a crime to be fought and breaks colonial economic influence.

workers-nation.rationale: Aflaq rejected class divisions and international class solidarity in favour of national unity.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Ba'th text claims civic rights for women but also treats the family as the national cell; Young Egypt was moralist, so a mild yes.

ban-interest.rationale: Ba'th Economic Article 10 bans usury between citizens and creates one state bank.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The Ba'th text defines Arabs by language, not race, so segregation is not central, though a minority admired Nazi race laws.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Aflaq rejected class struggle as divisive and held that all Arab classes shared interests against foreign capital, so the state is not a class tool.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The Ba'th text nationalises natural resources; production for national strength implies expansion.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Ba'th requires Arabic and Arab national education, and Arab by language is Arab.

elite-replacement.rationale: No documented belief in this conspiracy as a demographic claim.

proportional-representation.rationale: The Ba'th constitution promises genuine elections but no electoral system, and the fascist-style groups disliked party parliamentarism.

national-mission.rationale: Expansionist and missionary claims about the Arab nation; Young Egypt claimed Egypt's religious culture was superior to Europe's.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The movements defended family tradition; Ba'th text claims equal civic rights but not structural critique.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Ba'th text vows to fight corruption and Young Egypt attacked the Wafd and the old elite.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Some admired Nazi policies, but no documented eugenic programme.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Both Ba'thist regimes were police states and nothing in the doctrine imagines prosecuting the security services for past abuses.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Opposite of the interventionist state the Ba'th constitution describes.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The Ba'th text defines Arabs by language so intermixture was not condemned, though a Nazi-admiring strand might differ.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Ba'th text promises equality before law but only for loyal citizens; fascist-style views were hierarchical.

socialism-one-country.rationale: The Ba'th text is nationalist-first; its socialism serves Arab nationalism, not world revolution.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Arab nationalists regarded Israel as colonial, and the Ba'th text calls colonial settlement hostile.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Ba'th text promises unified legislation and combats sectarian particularism.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The Ba'th constitution calls freedom of religious affiliation sacred, though an Islamist-leaning strand might differ.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: A Muslim and Arab nationalist movement has no tradition of this cause; inferred from its absence in every source read.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Education is national; religious instruction is not covered.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Inferred from the strong-state outlook against foreign enemies.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Aflaq's party legitimacy rested on acting for the common good, not elections.

trade-surplus.rationale: Ba'th text has the state balance imports and exports and protect national production.

population-transfer.rationale: Ba'th text expels those who emigrated for colonial purposes; broader transfers not documented.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The Ba'th text prescribes struggle and fascist groups used force.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social-Darwinist strain in fascism glorifies struggle between peoples.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: One-party outlook supports outlawing rivals who challenge the order.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: A republican concept not found in the sources; Aflaq's party-guaranteed liberty tolerates unchecked power in the party's hands.

separated-powers.rationale: The Ba'th text promises an independent judiciary but also party supremacy, so weak support for checks.

vanguard-party.rationale: Aflaq's vanguard party dictated what was right even against majority opinion.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Ba'th condemns unjust distribution but gives national, not class, priority.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Ba'th guarantees a minimum holding of real estate to everyone, so ownership is favoured, but not this policy.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Class cooperation and national mobilisation would limit strikes, though Ba'th promises free unions.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The Ba'th text attributes poverty to unjust distribution and foreign domination.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Ba'th text opposes tribal, racial and sectarian particularism as a threat to national unity.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices filled by lot contradict the leader principle and elite-party rule that define the type.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Authoritarian practice and a doctrine of party above rights.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 11 has the state supervise internal and foreign trade, which fits setting maximum prices for essentials.

party-controls-media.rationale: Aflaq's party-led state; Ba'th text limits press freedom by national interest.

party-commands-army.rationale: Neo-Ba'th officers politicised the army, though control by party was disputed.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Ba'th text restricts civil rights to loyal citizens of Arab descent.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: No source covers it; the Ba'th text's worker-friendly tone leans for, but party elites in practice held privileges.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Ba'athism rests on a vanguard party that dictates the right line to members, and the paramilitary movements demanded obedience.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Ba'th aims at merging Arab states into one; pooling sovereignty within Arab world fits, though the EU as such is not discussed.

head-commands-forces.rationale: A leader-centred movement puts armed forces under the chief; Futuwwa and Green Shirts were organised around leaders.

church-by-bishops.rationale: An Islamic-world movement has no stake in episcopal church government; no position documented.

clerical-rule.rationale: Aflaq wanted Islam out of the state, and Young Egypt was nationalist not clerical.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Ultranationalists and militarists would reject national defeatism in wartime; Futuwwa trained youth for national war.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Young Egypt attacked 'anti-Islamic' entertainment and cinemas.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Inferred from the personalist presidencies of Assad and Saddam Hussein, though the 1947 text itself is silent.

recall-officials.rationale: Inferred: removal of leaders by voters conflicts with leader-led, anti-parliamentary politics.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Anti-colonial but Axis-seeking; Ba'th favoured non-alignment.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Ba'th forbids renting for others' use; Econ Art 8 forbids exploitative renting but does not abolish it.

people-in-arms.rationale: Futuwwa and Green Shirts armed youths; but states kept professional armies.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Young Egypt had an agrarian element in its infobox but other strands were urban student movements; split.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The Ba'th text aims to unite all Arabs in one state; Sykes-Picot borders were hated.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Anti-intellectualism is noted but the movements were led by students and officers, so adherents are split.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Ultranationalism asserts Arab superiority; Young Egypt claimed Egypt's religious culture was superior.

death-penalty.rationale: Ba'thist regimes executed political opponents and the party held that struggle justified force.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Inferred from Young Egypt's moral campaigns against 'anti-Islamic' entertainment; the Ba'th text calls for equal civic rights for women but nothing on curricula.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: No documented position; the Ba'th text wants a national Arab education but is silent on evolution.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Young Egypt attacked cinemas, gambling, alcohol and 'anti-Islamic' entertainment, so restricting pornography follows.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Arab identity by language and belonging; descent-based nationhood.

minority-language-support.rationale: The Ba'th constitution makes Arabic the official language of state and schooling and opposes particularism.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th text's call for unified legislation and a fight against sectarian particularism.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mass mobilisation, uniformed youth drill and cult of the leader prize conformity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th text abolishing foreign concessions and breaking economic influence of colonial powers.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Ba'th text pairs political independence with breaking foreign economic influence, and Young Egypt wanted economic independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Ba'th constitution promises a constitution with real elections but names no drafting body; fascist-style groups disliked assemblies.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Aflaq treated liberty as party-guaranteed; authoritarian development.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Not documented; anticolonial tilts to reparations, nationalist to self-reliance.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the aim of national military superiority and independence.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Plebiscites confirmed Ba'thist presidents in practice, but no doctrine on how a head of state is chosen.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 10 creates a single state bank issuing the currency, under government control.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Pan-Arab and expansionist claims over Arab land make trading territory for peace unacceptable.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 9 states that property and inheritance are natural rights limited by the national interest.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Aflaq admired some Marxist analysis but the movements were anticommunist and had no settled view on this Marxist debate.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Anachronistic; no documented environmental regulatory stance.

collective-defense.rationale: Pan-Arab solidarity and the aim of one Arab state imply an attack on one Arab state concerns all.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Arab nationalists held that territory taken from the Arab homeland by outside powers was held unlawfully, and the Ba'th text voids treaties infringing sovereignty.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Aflaq wanted Islam kept out of state governance while Young Egypt valued religious elements; split.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Leaders of these movements were party leaders, not symbols above politics.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Pan-Arab unity is the party's central aim and the text rejects regional particularism.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The Ba'th text calls for a single political and economic unit with unified legislation, though administration would be decentralised.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Ba'thist regimes cultivated leader cults but did not claim divine descent for the ruler.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The Ba'th text calls current wealth distribution unjust, so a regressive flat tax is unlikely to appeal.

character-from-environment.rationale: No documented view; nationalist and racial strands suggest innate nature, others stress education.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Authoritarian personalism; though Ba'th text promises independence of judiciary.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic for movements of the 1930s-40s; no documented position.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not documented; inferred from the preference for single-leader or single-party authority.

leader-cult.rationale: Arab fascism's leader worship; Ba'thist regimes developed personality cults.

equal-parenting.rationale: Not documented; the Ba'th text treats the family as basic cell but says nothing on custody.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Aflaq rejected class struggle outright, so he would have found it incoherent under any regime.

land-redistribution.rationale: Ba'th text caps agricultural holdings and abolishes feudalism.

refugee-return.rationale: Arab nationalists opposed Israel's creation and the article ties the movements' antisemitism to 1948; return of displaced Arabs followed from their claim.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The article states the movements pursued expansionist unified-Arab-nation aims, claiming lands for Arabs.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Ba'th text guarantees religious freedom; Islamist-leaning minority differ.

women-must-cover.rationale: Ba'th grants women civic rights, and secular strands opposed compulsion.

common-currency.rationale: The Ba'th text treats Arab territory as one political and economic unit, which implies a single currency.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The first principle of the 1947 Ba'th constitution and Gen. Art. 6 aim to unite all Arabs in one state.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The Ba'th text opposes tribal, racial and sectarian particularism and sets Arabic as sole official language.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The article describes growing antisemitism after Israel's founding; adherents did not hold that Jews should seek equal rights in Arab lands.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Aflaq rejected dialectical materialism as the sole truth and put the nation, language and spirit at the centre.

ban-cartels.rationale: No documented position on competition law; state ownership of major industry makes the issue moot.

no-bailouts.rationale: Not documented; state control of the economy could cut either way.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Inferred from an anti-liberal, plebiscitary outlook; but the Ba'th text promises an independent judiciary.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Ba'th text grants women full civic rights but does not call for quotas; the movements were male-led and traditional.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Young Egypt promoted buying only Egyptian goods and opposed foreign-owned factories.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; protectionists would reject binding trade rules, yet labor protections are in the Ba'th text.

moral-incentives.rationale: The Ba'th text makes work a national duty, and Futuwwa taught sacrifice for the nation.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Young Egypt, Futuwwa and later officer-led Ba'th factions pursued paramilitary and coup action to seize power.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Ba'th text opposes feudalism; Young Egypt, though, courted the king, so support is moderate.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Ba'th Educ. Art. 1 requires education with a national Arab character connecting students to Arab history.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Ba'th text calls colonialism a criminal enterprise to be fought by every means (First Principle).

patriotic-education.rationale: Ba'th Educ. Art. 1 requires national character in education and Futuwwa drilled schoolchildren in loyalty to the Arab nation.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not applicable to these movements; no documented stance.

public-money-creation.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 10 creates one state bank to issue currency.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Aflaq's view of capitalism was that it was foreign-linked and unjust, but he left no theory of its crises.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Inferred from the expansionist aims of Shawkat's Arab nation, not a stated claim about former empires.

delink-world-market.rationale: The Ba'th text breaks foreign economic influence but still seeks trade under state supervision.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Marxist theory Aflaq did not adopt; inferred from rejecting class analysis.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Statist nationalist ideology; the Ba'th text limits freedoms by the national interest.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Ba'th text lists freedoms but subordinates them to the Arab national interest.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Ba'th Foreign Art 3 cancels treaties infringing sovereignty.

elective-rulers.rationale: Aflaq's party-guaranteed rule and the leader principle do not rest on elections, though the text promises genuine elections.

minority-veto.rationale: A leader principle and mass movement discipline reject veto power for dissenters.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Not documented; adherents backed coups against governments they judged colonial or reactionary, yet defended their own rulers.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The movements attacked parliamentary factionalism, though the Ba'th text promises elected representation.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Nothing in the sources; no documented position.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Nothing in the sources; no documented position.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Not documented; the Ba'th text gives the state, not the rich, the duty of social provision.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Mass mobilisation and active commitment are central; withdrawal is the opposite of the movements' ethos.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Not documented, though Young Egypt condemned cinemas as morally harmful.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: A Gramscian claim not in the sources; Aflaq rejected class analysis.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: The Ba'th text condemns colonialism and foreign economic influence, abolishing concessions, which presumes outside extraction.

native-born-offices.rationale: Ba'th Educ. Art. 5 reserves teaching posts for Arab citizens and civil rights go to loyal citizens on Arab soil.

party-own-road.rationale: Ba'athism was non-aligned and rejected Soviet direction; this Marxist-party question is inferred.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Young Egypt's Piastre Plan funded national industry from national savings rather than foreign capital.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The Ba'th text defines the Arab homeland by its borders and aims to reunify it, so territory lost to outsiders must be reclaimed.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Not documented; Arab nationalists were anticolonial, but ethnic and sectarian minorities were treated as part of the Arab nation.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Movements modelled on fascism and receiving Axis support would reject it.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: They were anticommunist, but would resist being equated with the fascism they imitated.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Not relevant to these movements; no documented position.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: No documented position; a heritage-minded nationalism leans for, but anticolonial movements toppled colonial symbols.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Aflaq called a constitutional democratic system unsuitable for Syria, favouring a form fitted to Arab conditions.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The neo-Ba'ath was officer-led and militarist; Rashid Ali's 1941 coup was a military mutiny per the sources.

paid-care-work.rationale: Not documented; the Ba'th text praises the family but proposes no pay for housework.

filial-duty.rationale: The Ba'th text calls the family the basic cell of the nation, protected by the state.

office-by-exam.rationale: Ba'th Educ. Art. 5 reserves teaching for Arab citizens but names no general civil-service exam.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The Ba'th text abolishes foreign concessions and Young Egypt opposed foreign-owned factories.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Inferred from the text's view of marriage as a national duty regulated by the state.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Binding delegates to voters conflicts with the leader principle and vanguard rule.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: The Ba'th text gives the state social security and control of economic life.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 5 limits holdings to what the owner can farm personally, but keeps individual tenure.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The Ba'th text promises an elected representative system, but the leader-led movements disliked parliaments.

single-official-language.rationale: Ba'th Gen. Art. 8 makes Arabic the official language of the state and of schooling.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Foreign concessions are abolished (Econ. Art. 4) and economic influence of colonial powers is to be broken.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: A statist, hierarchical nationalism has no equality-of-results doctrine for racial groups.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Inferred from Young Egypt's moral critique of imported entertainment and its buy-national drives.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The article describes the Sudanese RSF as fascist and supremacist, and Axis-backed Arab groups armed insurgency against the British; support for armed proxies fits.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Not documented; Ba'th non-alignment opposes bloc discipline, yet unity ambitions favour compelling Arab states.

corporate-influence.rationale: Inferred from Young Egypt's anti-capitalism and hostility to foreign companies.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Young Egypt rejected foreign influence entirely and accused rivals of collaboration with foreign powers.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Ba'th Social Art. 1 treats marriage and children as a national duty to be encouraged by the state.

residents-only-property.rationale: Not documented; the Ba'th text limits foreign ownership but is silent on local rules.

job-guarantee.rationale: Ba'th Social Art. 3 states that the state must guarantee each citizen employment.

democratic-peace.rationale: The movements rejected liberal democracy and glorified war.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Discipline, obedience and cult of the leader are core to the type.

non-intervention.rationale: The Ba'th text opposes foreign intervention in Arab lands but would unify Arab states, so absolute non-intervention is not held.

industrial-unions.rationale: The Ba'th text promises free unions for workers and peasants but not their structure.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The article describes growing antisemitism, translation of Mein Kampf into Arabic and the Farhud, indicating belief in a Jewish conspiracy among part of the movement.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: The Ba'th text makes marriage a national duty regulated by the state.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Press freedom was limited by the national interest in Ba'th doctrine; no right to information is documented.

local-production.rationale: Young Egypt's buy-Egyptian drive and its Piastre Plan to build a domestic factory favoured goods produced and bought at home, and Ba'th Econ. Art. 11 protects national production.

informal-organisation.rationale: The movements were disciplined, uniformed mass organisations.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The Ba'th text voids treaties that infringe Arab sovereignty.

religious-nation.rationale: Ba'th defines Arabs by language and belonging; the article says only some adherents were Arab-Islamic nationalists.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Anti-colonial nationalists rejected subordination to a leading power.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The Ba'th text treats the homeland as one economic unit, which opposes regional hoarding.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: The Ba'th text permits personal property and real estate for everyone while nationalising large production.

defeat-communism.rationale: Fascist-style movements were anticommunist, and Young Egypt's infobox lists anticommunism.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The Ba'th text has the state run education and abolishes private schools.

religion-illusion.rationale: Even secular strands like Aflaq's praised Islam as an expression of Arab genius; the movements were not Marxist.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Young Egypt was anti-capitalist; Aflaq saw capitalism as foreign domination.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: The Ba'th text grants women civic rights by law with no link to economic transformation.

socialized-care.rationale: The Ba'th text calls the family the basic cell of the nation, so care stays in families.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred from the Ba'th text making Arabic the official language and stressing national character.

treaties-binding.rationale: Ba'th voids treaties that infringe Arab sovereignty but is silent on treaties with national minorities.

cooperative-communities.rationale: The Ba'th text centres on one unified Arab state with state-owned major industry, not small self-governing communes.

majority-settlement.rationale: Both Ba'thist regimes pursued Arabization of minority regions per the sources.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Ba'athism was a socialism fitted to Arab nationalism, rejecting Marxism and liberal capitalism alike, and the fascist type is a self-styled third way.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Expansionist claims to a greater Arab nation rest on historical unity.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The article records antisemitism but I found no source on Holocaust denial in the interwar movements, which predated it.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Inferred from the movements' morally conservative campaigns against vice.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Aflaq rejected pluralism and Ba'thist regimes were police states; Egypt banned Young Egypt's paramilitary only in 1938.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Young Egypt had religious elements, but secular Ba'th strands would not.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Ba'th text calls colonialism a crime and aims to break colonial economic influence.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Some adherents were Arab-Islamic nationalists, others secular, so a doctrine of obligatory jihad is split.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Aflaq wanted religion outside the state, so declaring secular rulers illegitimate is alien to the mainstream.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The movements stressed leadership and discipline over popular decision-making.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Aflaq denied class-based analysis and the movements were traditionalist.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Inferred from the movements' conservative moral campaigns; anachronistic.

assisted-dying.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from a conservative religious-moral outlook.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The Ba'th slogan combined unity, freedom and socialism, claiming a nationalism-socialism synthesis beyond left and right.

alienated-labor.rationale: A Marxist concept; Aflaq admired Marxist analysis only partly.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Young Egypt claimed Egypt's religious culture was superior to a godless Europe.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Some adherents were Arab-Islamic nationalists, others secular, so split.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Not documented; secular and Islamic strands differ.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Ba'th text goes beyond a regulated market to national ownership of major production.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Ba'th Internal Art. 8 makes military service compulsory.

rich-first.rationale: The Ba'th text calls current wealth distribution unjust and limits holdings.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Ba'athism rejected alignment with either Cold War bloc, but the interwar groups sought Axis support, so split by period.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Assadism enshrined family leadership but that was a later practice; the early movements did not state it.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The Ba'th text bans usury and sets one state bank, not user-owned banks.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The Ba'th text breaks foreign economic influence and voids concessions.

property-franchise.rationale: The Ba'th text promises genuine elections and equal civic rights, and the movements mobilised students and the poor.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminist claim outside the movements' discourse.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept; Aflaq rejected dialectical materialism as the sole truth.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The Ba'th text declares press freedom within the national interest and attacks wealth inequality, so mixed.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Ba'th text promises a constitution and independent judiciary, though leader-led practice ruled by decree.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Ba'th text defines Arabs by language and belonging, not race, though it limits civil rights to loyal citizens.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Not documented; Islamist-leaning adherents would restrict, secular ones not.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The article describes rising antisemitism and the Farhud; boycotts of Jewish commerce were a common Arab nationalist tactic.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Not documented; inferred from the leader-centred and anti-parliamentary outlook.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Aflaq praised Islam as Arab genius yet wanted it outside the state; Young Egypt was traditionalist; split.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: The Ba'th text calls the present distribution of wealth unjust and caps holdings.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred from the morally conservative, militarist outlook; anachronistic.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Aflaq opposed atheism and fundamentalism alike, though Syrian neo-Ba'athists were anti-religious.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The movements were militarist and security-minded.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: The Ba'th text opposes sectarian particularism and seeks unified legislation.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The Ba'th text makes the state guarantee social security.

term-limits.rationale: Ba'thist leaders held power long-term and the doctrine supports party continuity.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred from the leader-centred, anti-parliamentary outlook.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred from conservative religious-moral outlook; Ba'th text says nothing on religious offices.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Ba'th text grants women civic rights but treats the family as the basic cell of the nation; inferred traditional authority.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Ba'th civil rights go only to loyal citizens on Arab soil.

rent-control.rationale: Ba'th Econ. Art. 8 forbids renting property at others' expense and the state supervises the economy; inferred.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Futuwwa and the Green Shirts were defined by uniformed paramilitary youth organisation modelled on European fascist youth movements.

abolish-ip.rationale: Inferred from the statist, nationalist economics of the movements; no stance on patents is recorded.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic to the interwar movements; no basis for either side.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The movements were driven by ending British and French control, and the Ba'th constitution makes the struggle against colonialism a core provision.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Unaddressed by the interwar movements, which were antisemitic and nationalist; adherents would be split on the idea.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The 1947 Ba'th constitution bans exploitation of labour and limits property to what is not used to exploit others, and the movements were anti-capitalist.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The movements glorified militarism, struggle and force, so refusing to kill is contrary to their outlook.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Pan-Arab ultranationalism, as in the Ba'th constitution, presents the Arab nation as an eternal one with a continuous mission from ancient glory to the present.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Not addressed; fascist-style ideals of fixed gender roles make a constructionist view unlikely.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Inferred from the fascist family and gender ideals; feminist theory is anachronistic here.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Fascist-style movements like Futuwwa and the Green Shirts cultivated a cult of sacrifice and honoured those who fell for the nation.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The Ba'th constitution and fascist forms give politics a mission of struggle and national rebirth, but a good versus evil frame is inferred and varied between secular and Islamic strands.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The movements sought to gather all Arabs under one expansionist unity claim, not a cultural centre for a diaspora.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred from the stress on political unity, leadership and independence first, with cultural renewal following.

god-not-male.rationale: Not addressed; the Islamic-nationalist strands would reject the idea and the secular ones ignore it.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; the movements subordinated individual rights to the nation, so women's humanity is not the test for religion.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: The Young Egypt programme urged buying Egyptian and breaking foreign and minority control of the economy, and the movements turned antisemitic.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Pan-Arab unity into a single Arab state is the central aim, as in the Ba'th constitution.

independent-unions.rationale: Inferred from fascist forms in which a leader and a single movement control organised labour, as the Futuwwa and Green Shirts' structure shows.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The 1947 Ba'th constitution is socialist but national, and the movements stressed national unity over class power.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Inferred from the 1947 Ba'th constitution's state-run economy and social provision.

second-chamber.rationale: The movements were anti-parliamentary and leader-centred, so a second chamber beside an elected parliament is not a priority.

municipal-property.rationale: Inferred from state-nationalist economics, which place ownership with the national state or nation, not local communities.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Inferred from centralised leader-led politics and expansionist unity claims that rule out local assemblies holding decisions.

family-wage.rationale: Inferred from the movements' traditional family values and state-nationalist economics.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Not addressed; no principle of the movements points either way.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Not addressed; no principle of the movements points either way.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the authoritarian state that tolerates no untraceable activity.

online-anonymity.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from anti-parliamentary, authoritarian politics that demanded identifiable loyalty.

person-over-state.rationale: Fascist forms placed the nation and leader above the individual, who is trained into drilled national service.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Attitudes ranged from Islamic-nationalist to secular, but the 1947 Ba'th constitution speaks of Arab spiritual values, so the lean is slightly positive.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Inferred from the movements' centralised unity, so self-government is held at the centre's pleasure.

gm-crops.rationale: Anachronistic; the movements did not address agricultural technology.

dense-cities.rationale: Anachronistic; the movements did not address urban form.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Arab ultranationalism, influenced by German racial thinking, treated the Arab nation as one people with its own interests to defend.

racial-pride.rationale: The movements promoted Arab pride and, in parts, racial doctrine, and it was a central theme.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Militarism and expansionist unity claims were central, so wars beyond defence were accepted.

missingStatements.text: Young people should be organised into uniformed, drilled youth movements that train them for national service.
missingStatements.rationale: Futuwwa and the Green Shirts were defined by uniformed paramilitary youth organisation modelled on European fascist youth movements.

missingStatements.text: A nation under colonial rule may seek the backing of its rulers' rival great powers to win independence.
missingStatements.rationale: The movements sought Italian and German support against Britain and France; Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy backed Arab nationalism per the article.
missingStatements.declined: Seeking rival powers for independence is a historical tactic specific to the interwar period, not a lasting position other ideologies would answer.

notes: The category is contested: Jankowski calls Young Egypt 'playacting at paramilitarism', Hussein distanced himself from Hitler, and Saadeh denied fascism. Answers are for the Futuwwa and Young Egypt mainstream; the Ba'th 1947 constitution is more democratic and socialist than the fascist-style groups, so economic answers are lower confidence.
